question: The European automotive sector is becoming less competitive on the global market. EU car and car part manufacturers are dealing with both the digital and climate transition simultaneously, which is resulting in higher costs, falling demand and increased competitiveness from third-country companies.

Three German automotive suppliers have already announced their closure in Brotterode-Trusetal: Grammer, Marelli and BOS Plastics Systems1. Even Volkswagen has concerns about its future, specifically in relation to the tighter CO2 limits set to be imposed from 2025.

Volkswagen Group CEO Oliver Blume says that the conditions for developing electric vehicles are inadequate and that electrification is not keeping pace with the speed at which new regulations are being introduced2. 1.
Does the Commission recognise the connection between the issues faced by the EU’s motor industry and Green Deal policies?

Will the Commission take the automotive sector’s arguments into account and revise the regulations tightening CO2emission limits for new cars from 20253and will the Commission withdraw the proposed ban on registering cars with combustion engines from 2035?

Does the Commission recognise that in pursuing the objectives of the Green Deal we are becoming more reliant on Chinese technology and products, giving China unrestricted opportunities for economic development, as well as control and influence on EU policy?
answer: 1. Road transport is responsible for around a quarter of greenhouse gas emissions in the EU. In order to contribute to the EU’s objective set out in the European Climate Law (4) of becoming climate neutral by 2050, transport emissions will have to go down significantly in the coming decade.

The transformation towards zero-emission and digital mobility is ongoing, both in the EU and beyond, notably in the United States and China. In 2023, EU car production increased by over 10% and the EU recorded a EUR 90.6 billion new car trade surplus (5), with all major EU manufacturers registering record profits.

While transport electrification will cause structural shifts in employment between sectors, the transition will deliver a net positive impact on jobs across the economy. The Commission is committed to strengthening Europe as a business location, with a strong domestic manufacturing base and will continue to engage with industry and social partners to this end (6). 2.

The Commission will monitor the implementation of the CO 2 emission standards Regulation (7) for new cars and vans and report every two years to the European Parliament and to the Council on the progress made in the transition to zero-emission mobility. A review of the regulation is planned for 2026. 3.

The Commission is committed to defend EU industry from unfairly traded imports, including by using its trade defence instruments (8). An anti-subsidy investigation into electric vehicles imported from China is ongoing. The Commission is also acting to strengthen EU automotive value chains.

The Net Zero Industry Act (9) and Critical Raw Materials Regulation (10) will increase the competitiveness of the EU’s net-zero technology industrial base and ensure access to raw materials and key technologies for the green transition.
